opus-5.5.text:
Growing up in Guangzhou, I think my first real love was actually words before it was numbers. When I was little, my parents had a lot of books at home: classical poetry anthologies, the *Shiji*, the Four Great Classical Novels. I remember reading *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* far too young to understand the politics. I was just fascinated by the characters, by Zhuge Liang, by how strategy and loyalty and fate all got tangled together.

Classical poetry was a big part of it too. In school you memorize Tang and Song poems, and a lot of kids experience that as a chore. For me it felt almost like solving a puzzle. A *jueju* is so compressed: four lines, strict tonal patterns, parallelism, and somehow inside that tiny structure you get an entire landscape, or homesickness, or a whole dynasty falling. Looking back, I think that's the same thing that later drew me to mathematics: you have very tight constraints, and the beauty comes from what you manage to express within them.

History gave me something a bit different. Reading about the rise and fall of dynasties gave me a sense of scale, that ideas and institutions are built by people, and that they can change. Guangzhou itself is a city with a lot of history: the trading port, the Thirteen Factories, the place where many reformist and revolutionary ideas came in. Walking around the old neighborhoods, you feel that the city has always been a meeting point between China and the outside world.

So when people ask how a math person ended up caring about literature, I'd almost turn it around. The literature came first, and in some ways math was a continuation of it. Both are about finding structure and elegance, and about saying something true in the most economical way possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, that interest came from my family more than from school. I grew up in Guangzhou, and my grandparents and parents loved to recite classical poetry at the dinner table. My grandfather would quote Su Shi or Du Fu to make a point about something ordinary, like the weather or a bad grade. So poetry was never a museum object for me. It was the language people used when they wanted to say something that mattered.

I also had a habit as a kid of reading everything in the house, and we had shelves of history: Records of the Grand Historian, the Zizhi Tongjian, and a lot of popular retellings of the Three Kingdoms and the Tang dynasty. I remember being fascinated by how a historian like Sima Qian could write about an emperor and a bandit with the same seriousness. That taught me early on that structure and narrative matter, and that there is usually a human story underneath any system.

Later, when I moved toward mathematics, people assumed I had left all that behind. But I think the two things feel very similar to me. A good proof and a good classical poem both compress a great deal into very little, and both reward rereading. Chinese history also gave me a sense of long time horizons. When you grow up reading about dynasties rising and falling over centuries, you learn to be a bit patient with your own ambitions, and also a bit skeptical of anyone who says the current moment is unprecedented.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I think literature and history were connected for me. Literature made me curious about people’s lives—what they cared about, how they understood the world—and history gave those stories a larger context. Growing up in Guangzhou, there was also that relationship between the place around me and the much broader idea of Chinese culture. It’s hard to pinpoint a single moment when the interest began; I’d describe it more as a curiosity that gradually grew.

sol-6.1.text: Growing up in Guangzhou, Chinese literature and history felt very close to everyday life. There’s the language you speak at home, the stories people tell, and then the poems and texts you encounter at school. I think what drew me in was how literature could make the past feel personal. You could read something written hundreds of years ago and recognize an emotion—a longing for home, a friendship, a sense of uncertainty. That recognition made me curious about the history around it: who was writing, what their world was like, and why those words have stayed with us.
